correctness.rationale: The two scalar expectations at (1,±i)/√2 bound |h| for h=(F_21−F_12)/2. Schwarz–Pick then gives ρ≥2q/(1+q²) with q=t/2. The ordered critical nodes normalize to (−q,q); U_q interpolates there, and on |z|=1 its radius is (|2a_q cos θ−1|+|2a_q cos θ+1|)/2=1. Apply the scalar maximum principle to all unit-vector expectations. For any critical solution equality forces h(z)=z. Bounded radial limits exist, and summing the squared bounds on c±iz forces the half trace c to vanish. With diagonal D,−D and symmetric off-diagonal sum 2J, positivity of I+Im(F/z) on the circle, saturated at (1,i)/√2, gives a first-coordinate kernel equation Im(D/z)+i Im(J/z)=0. Thus D/z and J/z are real there. Fourier symmetry for a bounded analytic g with real g/z permits only g=α+βz+conj(α)z², β real. The node values make β=0 for D and J, and since q²<1 they give D=0 and J=a_q(1+z²). For larger separation the symmetric nodes (−s,s) have s>q. For every unit vector the scalar expectation of U_q is strictly below one in modulus in the interior, by the maximum principle and w(U_q(0))<1. Joint compactness on |z|≤q/s and the unit sphere gives a uniform strict bound, leaving room for nonzero perturbations vanishing at ±s.
residual_risks: No claim here about t=0 or t=2, unequal amplitudes, larger matrix size, or other domains. The finite boundary mesh does not establish uniqueness or strictness.

value.rationale: The example is the natural swapped-target test from numerical-radius interpolation, where a sharp scalar obstruction leaves many matrix entries apparently free. Proving that the supporting face constraints actually determine the whole analytic map is a substantive classification. The strict regime illustrates why uniqueness belongs to the threshold rather than merely to this choice of polynomial solution.
residual_risks: Value rests on full matrix rigidity, not on rediscovering a scalar Schwarz–Pick bound or a special case of the exact cost formula.
